summary: The Game Master describes the situation and asks what each character does.
A player states an intended action and approach.
The Game Master decides whether the action succeeds automatically, fails automatically, or needs a roll.
When a roll is needed, determine the relevant attribute, skill, defense, reaction, damage, or other mechanic.
Apply situational modifiers to produce an effective target number.
Roll the dice and compare the result with the target number or opposing result.
Apply consequences in the fiction, update resources, and continue.
core_play_loop.important_principle: Do not roll for routine actions with no meaningful uncertainty or consequence. Roll when the outcome matters.
player_responsibilities: Describe goals and methods rather than merely naming skills.
Know the character's most-used skills, defenses, damage, HP, FP, and disadvantages.
Help maintain the agreed campaign tone.
game_master_responsibilities: Define campaign limits before character creation.
Select which optional rules and supplements are active.
Set fair modifiers based on circumstances.
Control non-player characters and the world.
Avoid making every scene a roll or every problem a combat.

campaign_setup.why_it_matters: GURPS is a toolkit. A campaign becomes playable when the Game Master narrows the toolkit to a specific genre, power level, technology level, realism level, and approved set of traits.

session_zero_checklist.question: Who are the heroes, what do they do, and why do they stay together?
Is this realistic, cinematic, horrific, heroic, comedic, gritty, or mixed?
What technology exists, and what equipment is normally available?
Do magic, psionics, divine powers, superscience, or superhuman abilities exist?
How many character points build a starting hero?
How many points may come from disadvantages and reduced attributes?
Which advantages, disadvantages, skills, powers, and templates are approved, restricted, or forbidden?
Will the game use basic combat, tactical maps, hit locations, bleeding, harsh injury, cinematic options, or a selected subset?
How much emphasis is placed on reaction rolls, Influence skills, research, mysteries, status, wealth, and organizations?
Which themes are welcome, should remain off-screen, or are excluded?

suggested_starting_point_ranges.note: The GM should tightly control severe disadvantages and niche competence.
A common range for capable but still human-scale protagonists.
Requires clearer niche protection and stronger campaign limits.
Use templates, power frameworks, and careful GM review.

campaign_setup.range_note: These are practical orientation ranges, not mandatory official tiers. The Game Master sets the actual budget.

character_creation.overview: Build the person the campaign needs by spending a fixed character-point budget. Costs are positive for beneficial traits and negative for disadvantages or reduced capabilities.
recommended_order: Write a one-sentence concept and party role.
Confirm the campaign point budget, disadvantage limit, and allowed sources.
Set the four basic attributes.
Adjust secondary characteristics only when the concept needs them.
Choose social background, languages, cultural familiarity, wealth, status, and technology familiarity.
Choose advantages and perks that define exceptional capabilities.
Choose disadvantages and quirks that will genuinely appear in play.
Buy the skills the character uses professionally and under pressure.
Select equipment and calculate encumbrance, defenses, and damage.
Audit the sheet for legal costs, campaign fit, and obvious capability gaps.

basic_attributes.name: Intelligence
governs: Most mental, social, technical, and magical skills

basic_attributes.name: Health
governs: Resistance to unconsciousness, death, disease, and poison

design_advice: Attributes affect many skills and should represent broad capability.
A narrow specialist often saves points by buying individual skills instead of raising a whole attribute.
Extreme attribute values should require GM approval because they reshape many subsystems.

entries.name: Hit Points
entries.meaning: Capacity to withstand injury before unconsciousness, death checks, and destruction thresholds.

entries.name: Will
entries.meaning: Mental resistance, self-control in some situations, and concentration under pressure.

entries.name: Perception
entries.meaning: Noticing hidden, distant, or subtle things.

entries.name: Fatigue Points
entries.meaning: Energy expended by exertion, extra effort, powers, deprivation, and some attacks.
Turn order, Dodge, and general quickness.
Ground movement in yards per one-second combat turn before encumbrance and other modifiers.

advantages.definition: Beneficial innate, learned, social, supernatural, or cinematic capabilities purchased with points.
examples_by_function: Social rank, reputation, contacts, or wealth
controls: Exotic and supernatural traits should exist only when the campaign permits them.
Enhancements can increase an advantage's cost and capability.
Limitations can reduce cost by imposing meaningful restrictions.

perks.definition: Small advantages that normally cost 1 point.

disadvantages.definition: Meaningful limitations that return points and must affect play.
controls: The Game Master sets a disadvantage limit.
A disadvantage that never matters is not a legitimate source of points.
Conflicting, disruptive, or campaign-breaking disadvantages may be forbidden.
Some mental disadvantages use a self-control roll when a character tries to resist.

quirks.definition: Minor personality traits or inconveniences, commonly worth -1 point each.

skills.definition: Learned capabilities based on an attribute and a difficulty category.

standard_point_progression.note: The exact starting level depends on difficulty and controlling attribute.
typical_pattern: 2 points raises it by one level from the 1-point level.
4 points raises it by one more level.
Each additional +1 usually costs 4 more points.

defaults.definition: Some skills may be attempted untrained from an attribute or related skill at a penalty.
limits: Not every skill has a default.
A default is not the same as owning the skill.
Training or familiarity requirements can still prevent an attempt.
Buying at least 1 point normally replaces reliance on the default.

specializations_and_familiarity: Some skills require a specific specialty.
Using unfamiliar equipment, culture, procedures, or models can impose penalties until familiarity is gained.
The GM should identify campaign-critical specialties before play.
skill_selection_advice: Buy the skills the character must use during danger, not only background hobbies.
Every adventurer benefits from perception, movement, communication, and survival-related competence appropriate to the setting.
Avoid spending most points on a single spectacular ability while leaving the character unable to participate in ordinary scenes.
Templates reduce analysis paralysis and protect party roles.

templates_and_lenses.template: A packaged set of required and optional traits representing an occupation, species, archetype, or role.
templates_and_lenses.lens: A smaller package layered onto a template to represent a subtype, specialty, origin, or variation.
templates_and_lenses.best_use: The GM can present approved templates and lenses so players choose among campaign-appropriate options without searching the entire rule library.

topics: Patrons, Allies, Contacts, Enemies, Dependents, and Duties
social_and_setting_traits.advice: These traits matter most when the campaign uses them consistently. The GM should explain which societies, organizations, and resource levels are important.

final_sheet_audit: Point total equals the campaign budget.
Disadvantages remain within the allowed limit.
All exotic, supernatural, cinematic, and social traits are approved.
Skill specialties and prerequisites are legal.
Equipment matches technology, wealth, legality, and availability.
The character can contribute to the party's main activity.
The character has a reason to cooperate with the other protagonists.

procedure: Choose the relevant attribute or skill.
Apply bonuses and penalties to produce effective skill.
Roll 3d6.
A result less than or equal to effective skill succeeds unless an automatic-failure rule applies.
A result above effective skill fails.
The difference is the margin of success or margin of failure.
success_roll.probability_note: Because 3d6 produces a bell curve, a one-point modifier near ordinary skill levels matters more than it would on a flat d20 roll.

critical_success: A natural 3 or 4 is always a critical success.
A natural 5 is a critical success when effective skill is at least 15.
A natural 6 is a critical success when effective skill is at least 16.
critical_failure: A natural 18 is always a critical failure.
A natural 17 is a critical failure when effective skill is 15 or less.
Any roll at least 10 greater than effective skill is a critical failure.
automatic_and_critical_results.note: The official rules contain specific critical-result tables and situation-dependent effects that are not reproduced here.

modifiers.principle: Use the character's effective chance under the actual circumstances, not the unmodified sheet number.
common_sources: Visibility, noise, range, speed, posture, or footing
Injury, fatigue, shock, distraction, or unfamiliarity
Assistance, preparation, research, or favorable conditions

quick_contest.use_when: Two capabilities oppose each other and the result can be decided in one exchange.
procedure: Each side makes the appropriate success roll.
Compare margins of success; a successful roll beats a failed roll.
The greater margin wins.
Resolve ties according to the situation or repeat if the rules call for it.
examples: A social Influence attempt versus resistance

regular_contest.use_when: Opposition continues over time and repeated effort matters.
regular_contest.procedure: Both sides roll repeatedly under the relevant rules until one side achieves the required decisive result.

reaction_rolls.purpose: Determine an NPC's initial attitude or a group's response when it is not predetermined.
procedure: Roll 3d6.
Unlike success rolls, higher is better.
Apply reaction modifiers from appearance, reputation, status, behavior, circumstances, and relevant traits.
Consult the official reaction table for the response category.
reaction_rolls.important_distinction: A reaction roll is not the same as an Influence skill roll. Influence skills are deliberate attempts to change or secure an NPC response.

influence_rolls.summary: Use an appropriate social skill and the resistance procedure specified by the skill and situation. Success can produce a defined favorable response; failure can worsen the situation.
influence_rolls.advice: Roleplay the approach first, then roll when uncertainty remains. A strong speech does not excuse a missing capability, and a high skill does not force an NPC to violate impossible boundaries.

summary: Use Perception or a sensory specialty to notice things.
Use knowledge, professional, research, or investigative skills to interpret what was noticed.
The GM should provide obvious information automatically and reserve rolls for hidden, uncertain, or time-sensitive details.
On failure, avoid stopping the entire adventure; provide incomplete information, costs, delays, or alternate routes.

self_control_and_fright.self_control: Some mental disadvantages specify a self-control number. Roll 3d6 at or below that number to resist the disadvantage when resistance is allowed.
self_control_and_fright.fright_check: A frightening event may require a Will-based Fright Check with modifiers. Failure uses the official Fright Check procedure and table.

combat_scale.distance_unit: One yard per map hex in the standard tactical scale
turn_order: Act from highest Basic Speed to lowest.
Use DX and then the prescribed tie procedure when Basic Speed is tied.
The order normally remains fixed through the combat.

turn_procedure: At the start of the turn, choose a maneuver.
Perform the movement, attack, defense setup, readying, concentration, or other action allowed by that maneuver.
Active defenses usually occur during enemies' turns and depend on the maneuver already chosen.
Track shock, stun, posture, aim, readiness, ammunition, FP, HP, and ongoing effects.

core_maneuvers.name: Do Nothing
core_maneuvers.summary: Take no deliberate action; commonly required while mentally stunned.

core_maneuvers.name: Move
core_maneuvers.summary: Move up to the allowed distance without making a normal attack.

core_maneuvers.name: Attack
core_maneuvers.summary: Make one attack and usually take a limited step.

core_maneuvers.name: All-Out Attack
core_maneuvers.summary: Gain a stronger offensive benefit but forfeit active defenses until the next turn.

core_maneuvers.name: All-Out Defense
core_maneuvers.summary: Focus on survival through improved or multiple defenses, with no normal attack.

core_maneuvers.name: Aim
core_maneuvers.summary: Prepare a ranged attack to gain the weapon's Accuracy bonus on a later attack.

core_maneuvers.name: Evaluate
core_maneuvers.summary: Study a melee opponent to improve a later attack.

core_maneuvers.name: Feint
core_maneuvers.summary: Use a contest of combat skills to reduce an opponent's defense against a later attack.

core_maneuvers.name: Move and Attack
core_maneuvers.summary: Combine substantial movement with an attack at significant restrictions or penalties.

core_maneuvers.name: Ready
core_maneuvers.summary: Draw, pick up, reload, change grip, or otherwise prepare an item.

core_maneuvers.name: Concentrate
core_maneuvers.summary: Focus on a mental task, spell, power, or other concentration-based action.

core_maneuvers.name: Change Posture
core_maneuvers.summary: Stand, kneel, sit, crouch, lie down, or otherwise change posture.

core_maneuvers.name: Wait
core_maneuvers.summary: Declare a trigger and convert the maneuver into a specified action when that trigger occurs.

steps: Choose target, attack type, weapon, maneuver, and any options such as hit location or Deceptive Attack.
Calculate effective attack skill after all modifiers.
On failure, the attack misses unless a special rule says otherwise.
On success, the defender may attempt one legal active defense unless denied by surprise, maneuver, condition, or special effect.
If the defense succeeds, the attack is avoided or stopped.
If the defense fails, roll damage.
Apply armor divisor, Damage Resistance, penetrating damage, damage type, hit location, and other injury modifiers.
Apply shock, knockdown, stun, crippling, unconsciousness, death checks, and other consequences as required.

types.name: Dodge
types.base_formula: Basic Speed + 3, dropping fractions, then modified by encumbrance and circumstances

types.name: Parry
types.base_formula: Half the relevant weapon or unarmed combat skill, dropping fractions, + 3
types.use: Deflect or stop an attack with a weapon or limb.

types.name: Block
types.use: Stop an attack with a shield or suitable blocking object.

retreat.summary: A defender may often step away from an attacker to improve one active defense.
typical_bonus: +1 to most other Parries or Blocks
retreat.limits: Retreat requires legal movement and is limited by position, posture, terrain, and the number of retreats allowed.

restrictions: Stun, posture, encumbrance, visibility, surprise, and attack type can modify or prevent defenses.
Dodge can normally be attempted repeatedly; Block and repeated Parries have tighter limits or penalties.
Some attacks cannot be parried or blocked safely.

melee_options.deceptive_attack: For every -2 voluntarily taken to melee attack skill, reduce the target's active defense by 1.

hit_locations.summary: Targeting a specific body part imposes an attack penalty and can change injury, knockdown, crippling, or armor coverage.

rapid_strike.summary: Trade a significant skill penalty for multiple melee attacks; cinematic traits can reduce the penalty.

grappling.summary: A successful grapple limits movement and enables follow-up actions such as takedowns, pins, locks, or attempts to break free.

aim: A successful later attack can receive the weapon's Accuracy after sufficient Aim.
Additional aim time, bracing, scopes, sights, and equipment can add further bonuses under their rules.
Movement, injury, losing sight of the target, or interruption can spoil Aim.
common_modifiers: Rate of Fire and aiming aids

rapid_fire.summary: A successful burst scores one hit, plus additional hits for each full multiple of the weapon's Recoil by which the attack succeeds, up to the number of shots fired and subject to the exact rapid-fire rules.
rapid_fire.required_reference: Use the official Rate of Fire, Recoil, and Rapid Fire rules for exact bonuses and limits.

ranged_combat.range_table_note: The full Size and Speed/Range Table is intentionally not reproduced in this guide.

damage_process: Roll the attack's listed damage dice and modifiers.
Modify Damage Resistance for any armor divisor.
Subtract effective DR from basic damage.
Multiply penetrating damage by the damage type's wounding modifier and any hit-location modifier.
Round as directed by the rules to determine injury.
Subtract injury from HP and apply secondary effects.

common_wounding_modifiers.damage_type: Burning, corrosion, crushing, piercing, or toxic

secondary_effects.name: Shock
secondary_effects.summary: Recent injury can penalize DX- and IQ-based actions on the victim's next turn, normally to a maximum penalty of -4.

secondary_effects.name: Major Wound
secondary_effects.summary: A single injury greater than half the victim's HP can require a HT roll to avoid knockdown and stunning.

secondary_effects.name: Crippling Injury
secondary_effects.summary: Sufficient injury to a limb or extremity can disable it under the hit-location rules.

secondary_effects.name: Knockback
secondary_effects.summary: Some attacks can push a target based on damage and ST.

secondary_effects.name: Bleeding
secondary_effects.summary: Certain wounds can continue causing harm until treated.

hp_thresholds.effect: Basic Move and Dodge are reduced.
Roll HT at the start of each turn to remain conscious, subject to the full rules.

hp_thresholds.threshold: Each further full negative multiple of HP

hp_thresholds.effect: Usually represents total bodily destruction when the damage source can cause it.

fatigue.summary: FP represent short-term energy. Exertion, deprivation, heat, powers, extra effort, and some attacks reduce FP.
fatigue.low_fp: At very low FP, physical performance falls sharply. At 0 FP, additional exertion can cause HP loss and other consequences under the full rules.
fatigue.recovery: Rest normally restores FP, with the rate affected by conditions, traits, and the source of fatigue.

surprise_and_stun.surprise: A surprised character may be mentally stunned and unable to act effectively until recovery.
surprise_and_stun.mental_stun: A mentally stunned character normally must Do Nothing and make an IQ roll on later turns to recover.
surprise_and_stun.physical_stun: A physically stunned character has reduced defenses, may fall, and rolls HT to recover.

for_players: Choose a maneuver before reaching for dice.
Use cover, range, posture, retreat, and teamwork; standing still and trading attacks is dangerous.
Know one reliable attack and all active defenses before learning advanced options.
Retreat and All-Out Defense are often more valuable than another desperate attack.
for_game_masters: Start with basic combat and add one optional layer at a time.
Use morale, surrender, escape, and negotiation so fights do not always continue to death.
Avoid designing encounters solely by matching point totals; capabilities, equipment, positioning, and goals matter more.
Warn new players when a declared maneuver removes their defenses.

summary: Basic Move measures unencumbered ground speed in combat.
Carried weight produces encumbrance levels based on Basic Lift.
Terrain, posture, injury, fatigue, and movement mode further modify travel.

travel_and_time.summary: Outside combat, resolve movement at an appropriate time scale: seconds, minutes, hours, days, or longer. Use rolls only for hazards, navigation, pursuit, fatigue, or meaningful uncertainty.

stealth.summary: Stealth is usually opposed by Perception in a Quick Contest, modified for movement, cover, noise, light, distance, alertness, and equipment.

hazards.note: The Basic Set provides detailed procedures; the GM should use only hazards relevant to the campaign.

healing.natural_recovery: Under ordinary conditions, a daily HT roll can restore HP; traits, medical care, magic, technology, and campaign realism modify recovery.
healing.first_aid: First Aid can stabilize and restore limited HP according to technology level, time, and the official treatment rules.
healing.long_term_care: Physician skill, surgery, hospitalization, magical healing, regeneration, and advanced technology use their own procedures.

advice: The GM defines which equipment lists are available.
Starting wealth does not guarantee access to restricted or setting-inappropriate items.
Record ammunition, power cells, consumables, and carried weight when they matter.

technology_level.summary: Technology Level categorizes a society's general technological development. Characters can be familiar with a home TL and may suffer penalties or require skills when using unfamiliar technology.
technology_level.campaign_use: Set a baseline TL and identify superscience, anachronisms, restricted gear, and cross-TL access.

powers_magic_and_special_systems.principle: GURPS does not require one universal supernatural system. The Game Master selects a model that fits the setting.

approaches.name: Skill-based magic
approaches.summary: Spells are learned as skills, influenced by mana and prerequisites. The Basic Set introduces the framework; GURPS Magic greatly expands it.

approaches.name: Advantages as powers
approaches.summary: Build abilities from advantages, enhancements, limitations, power modifiers, and related skills. GURPS Powers expands this approach.

approaches.name: Psionics
approaches.summary: Commonly built as powers with abilities grouped by source and focus; specialized supplements add detail.

approaches.name: Divine or spirit abilities
approaches.summary: Can be represented by powers, granted advantages, learned rituals, reaction-based aid, or another approved subsystem.

approaches.name: Alternative magic systems
approaches.summary: GURPS supports many alternatives, including ritual, path, realm, syntactic, improvisational, and setting-specific systems.

approval_checklist: What shuts it down or resists it?
Does it cost FP, time, preparation, materials, or risk?
Which advantages, enhancements, limitations, skills, and power modifiers build it?
What is ordinary, exotic, supernatural, cinematic, or superscience in this setting?
How does the ability interact with mundane defenses and other powers?

social_resolution: Roleplay the request, leverage, threat, negotiation, or deception.
Determine what the NPC wants, fears, knows, and can legally or morally do.
Choose a reaction roll, Influence roll, contest, or automatic result.
Apply social traits, status, reputation, appearance, culture, language, and circumstances.
Translate the result into a believable response rather than mind control.
social_play_and_campaign_world.organizations: Patrons, Duties, Rank, Status, Contacts, Allies, Enemies, and Reputation can make institutions mechanically relevant.
social_play_and_campaign_world.wealth_and_resources: Wealth affects starting resources and often lifestyle or income. It does not automatically bypass law, scarcity, social permission, or campaign restrictions.
social_play_and_campaign_world.information_control: Separate what the player knows from what the character can establish through Perception, research, professional skills, contacts, or investigation.

spending_options: Learn new skills when training or experience justifies them.
Raise attributes or secondary characteristics with GM approval.
Buy new advantages when the story explains their acquisition.
Buy off disadvantages when play justifies the change.
Acquire social traits, contacts, rank, wealth, or powers through events.
advancement.training_and_justification: The GM decides whether points alone are sufficient or whether instruction, time, access, transformation, or an in-world event is required.
advancement.no_character_levels: GURPS has no mandatory class level. Growth is purchased directly in the traits that improve.

before_the_campaign: Set point totals and disadvantage limits.
Define technology, supernatural assumptions, and available gear.
Create an allowed-trait list or templates.
Select only the optional rules that support the intended experience.
Prepare a brief explanation of what competent characters should be able to do.
before_each_session: Review character disadvantages, duties, enemies, allies, and unresolved goals.
Prepare situations rather than a single mandatory plot path.
Record likely NPC motives and only the statistics that may be used.
Identify terrain, clues, resources, and consequences.
Have ordinary task modifiers and combat statistics ready.
during_play: State the stakes before an important roll when possible.
Use one roll to answer one meaningful question.
Prefer broad rulings over stopping play to search for an obscure modifier.
Record temporary rulings and verify them after the session.
Use reaction and morale rather than assuming every NPC fights irrationally.
Call for disadvantages when they matter, but do not use them solely to punish players.
after_play: Update relationships, resources, injuries, reputation, and campaign clocks.
Ask which rules added fun and which added friction.
Add or remove optional detail deliberately.

npc_design.principle: Most NPCs do not need complete point accounting.
minimum_stat_block: DR, HP, and FP when relevant

learning_profiles.note: These profiles are onboarding recommendations, not separate official editions.

use: GURPS Lite or pre-generated Basic Set characters
Basic attributes and a small approved skill list
Dodge, Parry, Block, DR, damage, HP, and FP

add: Aiming, cover, rapid fire, Deceptive Attack, and selected hit locations
One campaign-appropriate supernatural or technology subsystem

add_carefully: Full hit locations and armor coverage
Detailed visibility, range, speed, and posture
Detailed firearms, vehicles, survival, or technical rules

worked_examples.name: Ordinary success roll
worked_examples.setup: A character has Climbing-12. Rain and poor handholds impose -2.
worked_examples.result: Success by 2. The character climbs successfully with a margin of success of 2.

worked_examples.name: Failed success roll
worked_examples.setup: A character has Electronics Repair-11 and attempts a rushed repair at -3.
worked_examples.result: Failure by 4. The GM applies a consequence such as lost time, worsened damage, or the need for better tools.

worked_examples.name: Quick Contest
worked_examples.setup: An infiltrator rolls Stealth-13 against a guard's Perception-12.
worked_examples.result: The infiltrator wins the Quick Contest by 2 and remains unnoticed under the circumstances.

worked_examples.name: Basic melee attack
worked_examples.setup: A fighter has Broadsword-14 and takes -2 in situational penalties.
worked_examples.defense: The target has Dodge-9; roll 11, failure.
worked_examples.damage: The attack rolls 7 cutting damage. The target has DR 3, leaving 4 penetrating damage. Cutting's ×1.5 wounding modifier produces 6 injury.
worked_examples.result: The target loses 6 HP and may suffer shock or other effects depending on total HP and circumstances.

worked_examples.name: Deceptive Attack
worked_examples.setup: A duelist with Rapier-16 voluntarily takes -4 to attack.
worked_examples.calculation: Attack is made at effective skill 12, and the defender suffers -2 to the chosen active defense if the attack succeeds.
worked_examples.result: This trades accuracy for a better chance of getting past a skilled defense.

worked_examples.name: Reaction versus Influence
worked_examples.setup: The heroes approach a neutral official.
worked_examples.reaction_use: If the official's starting attitude is uncertain, the GM can make a reaction roll.
worked_examples.influence_use: If a hero then makes a specific request using Diplomacy, Fast-Talk, Intimidation, or another appropriate skill, resolve that deliberate attempt under the Influence rules.
worked_examples.result: Initial attitude and deliberate persuasion are related but distinct procedures.

preparation: Use a focused premise and pre-generated or template-based characters.
Put each character's three most-used skills, attack, damage, defenses, HP, and FP in a visible quick-reference box.
Choose basic combat and at most one optional rule layer.

teaches: A simple Perception or reaction roll
A Quick Contest such as Stealth versus Perception or Influence versus resistance

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to use every GURPS rule.
common_mistakes.correction: Choose the smallest rule set that supports the campaign, then add detail only when it improves play.

common_mistakes.mistake: Allowing players to search every published trait without campaign limits.
common_mistakes.correction: Use an approved list, templates, or GM-reviewed proposals.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing roll-low and roll-high mechanics.
common_mistakes.correction: Success rolls and defenses usually want low results; damage and reaction rolls generally want high results.

common_mistakes.mistake: Building characters independently before the campaign is defined.
common_mistakes.correction: Set premise, points, technology, powers, and roles first.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating disadvantages as free points.
common_mistakes.correction: Disadvantages must appear in play and shape decisions.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignoring active defenses.
common_mistakes.correction: A successful attack roll normally gives the target a separate defense roll.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using point total as the only measure of combat difficulty.
common_mistakes.correction: Equipment, skill concentration, defenses, mobility, terrain, surprise, objectives, and action economy dominate many encounters.

common_mistakes.mistake: Making every failed information roll stop the adventure.
common_mistakes.correction: Use costs, delays, partial clues, risk, or alternate paths instead of dead ends.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting optional realism surprise the players.
common_mistakes.correction: Declare harsh injury, bleeding, ammunition, encumbrance, survival, and social-detail rules before play.

quick_reference.one_line_core: Roll 3d6 at or below effective skill; in combat, a successful attack is normally followed by the target's active defense, then damage minus DR and injury modifiers.
remember: Lower is better for success and defense rolls.
Higher is generally better for damage and reaction rolls.
Choose a maneuver every combat turn.
A successful attack is not automatically a hit.
DR reduces damage before most wounding multipliers.
GURPS is configured by the campaign, not played with every published option.

glossary.definition: Roll three six-sided dice and total them.
A Dodge, Parry, or Block roll made in response to an attack.
A beneficial trait purchased with character points.
A ST-derived measure used for lifting and encumbrance.
The accounting unit used to build and improve characters.
Protection subtracted from incoming basic damage before injury is calculated.
A penalized untrained way to attempt certain skills.
A limiting trait that returns character points and must affect play.
The final target number after all modifiers.
Fatigue Points, representing short-term energy.
Hit Points, representing capacity to withstand injury.
Effective skill minus the dice result on a successful roll.
The action category chosen for a one-second combat turn.
A small advantage, usually costing 1 point.
Opposed rolls where the better margin wins.
A minor disadvantage or defining behavioral detail, commonly worth -1 point.
A 3d6 roll where higher is better, used to determine an NPC's response.
A learned capability based on an attribute and difficulty.
A package of traits representing a role, occupation, species, or archetype.
Technology Level.
A multiplier applied to penetrating damage to determine injury.
